docs.title: Phantom Architecture
docs.text:
A catalog of twenty-five designs that never left the page.

The buildings in this catalog share no common style, no era, and no scale. What they share is a single strange property: they were drawn, modeled, staked out, and sometimes begun — but they were never built. Some were stopped by money, some by politics, some by war, some by physics. A few were overruled by the architect's own death. Most were simply too large an idea for the world that held them.

They are phantoms. They exist in plates, in sketches, in wooden models in museum basements. The drawing survives; the building never began.

The project is inspired by Philip Wilkinson's Phantom Architecture (2017). The cases are the well-known ones — Boullée's sphere, Tatlin's spiral, Wright's mile, Hadid's opera house — the canonical set that any such catalog must cover. The prose and the illustrations are new.

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
I. Visions before modernity

  • 1563 The Tower of Babel — Bruegel
  • 1457 Sforzinda — Filarete
  • 1487 Ideal City — Leonardo da Vinci

II. The Enlightenment

  • 1784 Cenotaph for Newton — Boullée
  • 1775 Royal Saltworks at Chaux — Ledoux
  • 1779 Royal Palace at Westminster — Soane

III. Into the industrial

  • 1914 Città Nuova — Sant'Elia
  • 1908 Hotel Attraction — Gaudí
  • 1922 Chicago Tribune Column — Loos

IV. Revolution

  • 1919 Monument to the Third International — Tatlin
  • 1929 The Metropolis of Tomorrow — Ferriss

V. The modernist scale

  • 1925 Plan Voisin — Le Corbusier
  • 1932 Broadacre City — Wright
  • 1956 The Illinois / Mile-High — Wright

VI. Monuments of power

  • 1933 Palace of the Soviets — Iofan
  • 1937 Volkshalle, Germania — Speer

VII. Post-war utopias

  • 1960 Dome over Manhattan — Fuller
  • 1960 Tokyo Bay Plan — Tange
  • 1961 Fun Palace — Price
  • 1964 Walking City — Archigram
  • 1964 Plug-in City — Archigram
  • 1969 Continuous Monument — Superstudio

VIII. Late phantoms

  • 1989 Mega-City Pyramid — Shimizu
  • 1994 Cardiff Bay Opera House — Hadid
  • 2007 Crystal Island — Foster

docs.title: A note on illustrations
docs.text:
Every entry carries a schematic drawing rendered to SVG in a unified blueprint style: an elevation for most, a plan or section where that says more. These are not photographic reconstructions. Each gives the essential form and something to measure it by — a human figure where one would be visible, otherwise a familiar building drawn at the same scale. Where the original drawing is precise (Boullée), the SVG approximates it; where the original is a collage or a mood-piece (Archigram, Ferriss), the SVG imposes more structure than the source strictly permits.

The generator is deterministic and lives in scripts/generate_illustrations.py. Running it produces identical output each time, which is the minimum a catalog owes its reader.

See Method & sources for the approach and the shared bibliography.

Begin: The Tower of Babel →

docs.title: What the entries try to do
docs.text:
Each entry aims to be read in ten minutes, with enough information to:

  1. Locate the project in time, space, and the career of its architect.
  2. Describe what the project was meant to be, including approximate scale.
  3. Explain why it did not get built, or — in the few partially built cases — why it stopped.
  4. Offer a short counterfactual: what would it have meant, for its city and for the discipline, had the building gone up.

The fourth section is interpretive and is marked as such in the prose. The first three stay close to the shared historical record.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
The catalog draws on the standard secondary literature. For a single source that covers most of the cases here, the best starting point is:

  • Wilkinson, Philip. Phantom Architecture. Simon & Schuster, 2017.

For individual projects, the following were consulted either directly or via the references cited in them:

  • Boullée — Jean-Marie Pérouse de Montclos, Étienne-Louis Boullée, 1969; and Boullée's own Architecture, essai sur l'art (posthumous).
  • Ledoux — Anthony Vidler, Claude-Nicolas Ledoux, 1990.
  • Tatlin — Camilla Gray, The Russian Experiment in Art, 1971; and the Christina Lodder literature on Constructivism.
  • Le Corbusier — Urbanisme (1925) for the primary-source presentation of Plan Voisin.
  • Wright — Neil Levine, The Architecture of Frank Lloyd Wright, 1996, for Broadacre and Mile-High.
  • Iofan & Speer — Sudjic and Jones, Architecture and Democracy (2001); Alex Scobie, Hitler's State Architecture (1990).
  • Archigram — Peter Cook (ed.), Archigram, 1972, reissued 1999.
  • Superstudio — Peter Lang and William Menking, Superstudio: Life Without Objects, 2003.
  • Hadid — Aaron Betsky and Patrik Schumacher, Zaha Hadid: The Complete Works, 2009.

Where dimensions are cited ("450 m," "2,004 m," "528 floors"), the figures are the ones the architects or their offices gave in their publications and competition submissions. They are usually the figures that appear on the drawings themselves. In a few cases the literature gives a range; where this happens the entry picks a widely-cited number and does not hedge.

docs.title: What the catalog does not do
docs.text:
• It does not reconstruct the buildings in three dimensions. Direction #4 in the project ideas page sketches what that would look like.
  • It does not attempt a complete bibliography per entry. The full references for any individual project run to dozens of items; that is a librarian's task.
  • It does not include unbuilt infrastructure (bridges, dams, tunnels) or unbuilt urban plans without architectural content (traffic schemes, zoning maps). The subject is the building as phantom.

docs.title: Illustrations
docs.text:
The SVG illustrations are generated programmatically from scripts/generate_illustrations.py. The drawings live in scripts/illustrations/, one module per part of the catalog. Each is a line drawing in a unified blueprint style: warm cream paper, near-black ink, hatching for shade. Scale is given by a 1.8-metre human figure where one would be visible, and otherwise by a familiar building drawn at the same scale and shown at its present-day height (the Eiffel Tower at 330 metres, for instance). The style is inspired by the line-drawings of Robert Venturi and Denise Scott Brown, and by the plates in Ackerman's Palladio — clean, diagrammatic, willing to sacrifice accuracy for legibility.

Where the original architect's drawings are famous in their own right (Bruegel's painting, Boullée's plate, Ferriss's charcoals, Hadid's paintings), the reader should seek out those sources. Wikipedia's Commons has public-domain reproductions of most.

docs.text:

docs.title: Project ideas
docs.text: This catalog is direction #1 of six sketched during the initial design session. The others live here as a record, in case a later mood calls for one of them.

docs.title: 1. Catalog of the unbuilt (this site)
docs.text:
A MkDocs-style catalog of ~25 real historical unbuilt buildings — each with architect, year, site, vital statistics, narrative of what it was, why it failed, and a short what-if. Schematic blueprint-style SVG elevations. Archival typography.

Status: built.

docs.title: 2. Phantom Architecture of the Internet
docs.text:
Same format, different subject: unbuilt or lost software systems. Xanadu. Engelbart's Augment. The Symbolics Lisp machines. Alan Kay's Dynabook. Project Juno. Plan 9's successors. Software's own cathedrals that were dreamed and never built, or built and lost. Technical kin to the quant work while preserving the book's spirit.

Effort: similar to this site. A weekend to a week.

docs.title: 3. Generative phantoms
docs.text:
LLM-seeded new unbuilt buildings in the voice of historical architects — Boullée writing a 2026 memorial, Tatlin drafting a cloud anchor for Shanghai. Manifesto + spec + SVG elevation, all generated. Fun; risks feeling shallow if the prose is thin.

Effort: a week for the generator, plus curation loop.

docs.title: 4. Three.js 3D walkthroughs
docs.text:
Pick four to six iconic unbuilt buildings and render each as a navigable 3D model the reader flies through — Boullée's Newton cenotaph at dusk, Tatlin spinning, Wright's mile rising out of Chicago. Weeks of work per building but genuinely impressive output.

Effort: one to two months for a meaningful set.

docs.title: 5. The impossible skyline
docs.text:
Pick one real city (Manhattan, Paris, Moscow) and layer every unbuilt proposal for that city onto an interactive map — Gaudí's hotel, Ferriss's pyramids, Le Corbusier's X-towers. The city as it would have been if every architect had gotten their way. Map + story + architectural history.

Effort: one to two months, primarily for the map UI and data collection.

docs.title: 6. Blend
docs.text:
Use direction #2 (internet phantom architecture) as the scaffolding, with direction #3 (generative phantoms) as an appendix. Real unbuilt software up front; generated "what would Engelbart propose now" at the back.

Effort: two to three weeks.

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text:
Direction #2 is the natural next step from this one — same tooling, same register, different subject matter. It also resonates with the quant project: software has its own cathedrals, dreamed and never built.

Direction #5 (the impossible skyline) is the most ambitious and probably the most compelling output. A natural follow-up after #2.

docs.title: Royal Saltworks at Chaux
docs.text: ArchitectClaude-Nicolas Ledoux (1736–1806) Designed1775 (half-circle); expanded to an ideal city plan c. 1804 Intended siteArc-et-Senans, between the forests of Chaux and the town of Salins Height / scaleIdeal city of approximately 2 km diameter; only the inner half-circle was built Statuspartially built — ideal city unrealised The built half-circle, with the Director's House at centre and workshops on the arc; the unbuilt half dashed

docs.title: What it was
docs.text:
In the 1770s the French Crown commissioned a new saltworks in Franche-Comté. The existing facility at Salins was running out of fuel — the forests around it had been felled to stoke its furnaces — and production needed to be moved closer to the still-wooded country around Arc-et-Senans, with the brine being piped across on a long aqueduct. Ledoux, royal architect, was given the design.

His built scheme is a half-circle. At the diameter, the Director's House stands on axis, an austere Palladian block. From the Director's House a colonnade faces outward, onto a gravelled court. Around the arc of the half-circle are eleven pavilions: workshops, crystallisation halls, and barracks for the workers. The walls are local stone, dressed in a stripped neoclassical vocabulary Ledoux made his own — plain ashlar, banded rustication, columns that look like they could be freshly quarried. The whole composition reads as a royal residence for industrial labour. Nothing in Europe looked like this in 1775.

This much was built between 1775 and 1779. It survives, on the UNESCO list, and can be visited.

What was not built is the rest. In the years after the Revolution Ledoux expanded the half-circle into a full ideal city — the Ideal City of Chaux — which he presented in engravings in 1804 in L'Architecture considérée sous le rapport de l'art, des mœurs et de la législation. The full plan extends the existing half-circle into a complete circle, and around the circle Ledoux arranged the social programme of an entire town: a Market Square, a Courthouse, a Cemetery (rendered as a hollow sphere — an echo of Boullée), a House of the Surveyor of the Loue River (rendered as a cylinder pierced by the river itself), and a House of Sexual Union (rendered as a phallic plan). Every building was a geometric figure whose form communicated its function. This is architecture parlante carried further than Boullée carried it: a city where you could navigate by the signature shape of each institution.

docs.title: Why it failed
docs.text:
The half-circle was built, and it ran. What stopped the larger scheme was the French Revolution. Ledoux was royal architect — he had designed the hated tax barriers of Paris, the propylées that ringed the city to collect the tax on goods entering it. In 1789 the barriers were his legal liability. He was imprisoned in 1793 and spent the Terror writing and drawing, narrowly escaping the guillotine. After his release he published the Ideal City of Chaux, fifteen years after the half-circle had been built and decades after the monarchy had ceased to commission anything. The ideal city was, by the time it was proposed, a proposal to a regime that no longer existed.

The saltworks themselves continued to operate until 1895, when the industry became uneconomic. The buildings fell into disuse, then into preservation. The phantom part of the project — the radial city around the half-circle — was never started.

docs.title: What-if
docs.text:
Chaux's built half remains the most complete early example of industrial buildings designed as architecture, rather than as sheds. If the full ideal city had been built, it would have been the first planned industrial community, fifty years before Robert Owen's New Lanark and seventy before Saltaire. It would also have been the most literal reading of architecture parlante ever constructed — a place where the buildings' forms named the buildings' functions without a word of signage.

The partial Chaux is eloquent in a way the complete Chaux could not have been. We have the built core, Palladian and austere, and around it the engraved plates of the unbuilt city — each building an idea, each idea rendered as a shape. The phantom half is easier to love than any realised ideal city has been.

Next: Royal Palace at Westminster →

docs.title: Cenotaph for Newton
docs.text: ArchitectÉtienne-Louis Boullée (1728–1799) Designed1784; plates preserved in the Bibliothèque nationale de France Intended siteParis; the cenotaph is notional, with no chosen lot Height / scaleHollow sphere of approximately 150 m diameter, set on a triple-stepped cylindrical base Statusunbuilt — a thesis in drawing A hollow sphere on a triple-tiered base, cypress trees at the perimeter

docs.title: What it was
docs.text:
Sir Isaac Newton died in 1727. In 1784, fifty-seven years later, a Parisian architect in his middle sixties sat down to design a tomb for him. Étienne-Louis Boullée had by this point all but stopped building. The school where he taught — the Académie royale d'architecture — had given him room to produce what he called "architecture parlante," speaking architecture, buildings whose form carried their meaning directly. The cenotaph for Newton is the most extreme of these.

The design is a hollow sphere of approximately 150 metres in diameter, sitting on a base of three low cylindrical tiers each planted with cypress trees. The entrance is a low arched portal in the base. A visitor entering the portal steps into the sphere's enormous interior. The sphere's inner surface is pierced with small apertures, which let in pinpoints of daylight. These pinpoints, against the blackness of the sphere's interior, resolve into the constellations of the night sky. The visitor stands at the centre of a perfect representation of the cosmos, at noon, in perpetual night. In the middle of the sphere, a small sarcophagus holds Newton's name.

Boullée described the intention directly: "O Newton! ... I conceived the idea of surrounding thee with thy discovery, and thus, somehow, surrounding thee with thyself." The sphere is a monument to the man by being a monument to the thing the man explained.

docs.title: Why it failed
docs.text:
The cenotaph was never meant to be built. Boullée presented it as a proposal in the same way that a later architect would present a competition board: it is a demonstration of principle. The sphere's structural problem is trivial — a 150-metre sphere of masonry cannot stand against its own weight, and even in reinforced concrete it would require engineering that Boullée's century had no access to. This was obvious to Boullée, and it was obvious to his contemporaries. The drawings were received at the Académie as a theoretical work.

What the cenotaph did do, more effectively than many built buildings, was teach. Boullée's plates circulated across Europe through engravings. The combined image of a vast primitive volume and a tiny human figure — the image that the engravings made inescapable — entered the architectural vocabulary and stayed. Every colossal twentieth-century monument, from the Palace of the Soviets to the Volkshalle to the Atomium, is working within terms Boullée established.

docs.title: What-if
docs.text:
If the cenotaph had been built, Paris would have a landmark in the lineage of the Panthéon and the Eiffel Tower — a structure whose silhouette would have dominated the city's skyline for generations. The interior experience — a reconstructed sky in permanent darkness, with Newton's sarcophagus at the centre — would have been something no other building delivered. It would have been visited the way the Hagia Sophia is visited: as an interior that changes you while you stand in it.

What the cenotaph actually did was more useful than what a built version could have done. By demonstrating that architecture could be about a single idea taken to an extreme, Boullée gave every architect after him permission to be extreme. The twentieth-century modernism that followed the Beaux-Arts — Le Corbusier, Wright, Mies — is unthinkable without the specific courage of Boullée's sphere. A phantom can teach more than a monument.

Next: Royal Saltworks at Chaux →

docs.title: Royal Palace at Westminster
docs.text: ArchitectJohn Soane (1753–1837) Designed1779; the Gold Medal thesis at the Royal Academy Intended siteA notional site at Westminster, chosen to permit ceremonial siting along the Thames Height / scalePrincipal block with six-column portico, flanking wings, crowning dome; no specified overall dimensions, but scaled for a royal court Statusunbuilt — student thesis Palladian main block with hexastyle portico, flanking wings, and low central dome

docs.title: What it was
docs.text:
John Soane was twenty-five when he drew the Royal Palace. He had just finished his studies under George Dance the Younger, and was preparing for the Royal Academy Gold Medal — the student prize that funded the winner's travel to Italy. The programme for 1779 was a royal palace. Soane's scheme won.

His design is a Palladian composition at enormous scale. The principal block is a three-storey rectangular mass crowned by a low central dome and approached by a six-column portico in the Corinthian order. The portico carries a pediment containing an allegorical relief of Britannia receiving the homage of the arts and sciences. Wings extend on either side, each terminating in its own pedimented block, connected to the main mass by low colonnades. The whole composition reads across the Thames as a horizontal bar with a central dome, anchored by two symmetrical flankers. The plan provides for royal apartments on a piano nobile, state reception rooms, a throne room, a chapel, and the necessary household offices below.

Soane won the medal, took the Italian travel grant, and spent the next two years in Rome, Naples, and Sicily. When he returned to London he became one of the great architects of his century: the Bank of England, Sir John Soane's Museum at Lincoln's Inn Fields, Pitzhanger Manor, and a series of remarkable country houses. He did not design another royal palace, and no one commissioned one. The Westminster palace stayed in his drawers.

docs.title: Why it failed
docs.text:
There was no client for a royal palace in Westminster in 1779 or at any subsequent date. George III lived at Buckingham House (which was eventually rebuilt as Buckingham Palace, though not by Soane). His successors never required a second palace, and the budget for building one on the scale Soane proposed would not have survived a Commons vote. The design was, and remained, an academic exercise.

The Royal Academy thesis programmes of the late eighteenth century routinely produced projects of this kind — buildings too grand, too expensive, too politically unthinkable ever to build, drawn with the full rigour of a real commission. The students were being trained in composition, not in procurement. Soane's Palace is one of hundreds of such drawings produced across Europe in that half-century. Most of them are now lost. Soane's survives because he kept everything; his museum at Lincoln's Inn still holds the original sheets.

docs.title: What-if
docs.text:
A Westminster palace on this scale, had it been built, would have reorganised the south bank of the Thames. The axis of the river, today anchored by the Houses of Parliament (Barry, 1840–70), would instead have been anchored by Soane's dome and colonnades. The political geography of London would have been different: a monarch resident at Westminster rather than at Buckingham, with the Commons meeting in a less prepossessing hall.

The more interesting what-if is what Soane became because the palace was not built. Having failed to build a palace in his youth, he spent his career building the interiors of the Bank of England — the stock office, the consols office, the reduced rotunda — which are perhaps the most inventive interior spaces any English architect has produced. The Bank's later demolitions in the 1920s make the Bank nearly as phantom as the Palace. Soane, strangely, is an architect whose best work is half-gone and half-never-built.

Next: Città Nuova →

docs.title: Città Nuova
docs.text: ArchitectAntonio Sant'Elia (1888–1916) Designed1912–1914, exhibited as the Nuove Tendenze show, Milan, May 1914 Intended siteMilan, or any modern city; the scheme was generic Height / scaleMulti-level setback towers; elevated and subterranean roadways; no fixed dimensions Statusunbuilt — Sant'Elia killed at Monfalcone, 10 October 1916 A setback industrial tower with external elevator shafts and an elevated roadway

docs.title: What it was
docs.text:
Antonio Sant'Elia was twenty-five when he drew the Città Nuova. He had set up his own studio in Milan, was working on minor commissions for banks and apartment buildings, and was spending his evenings at the Caffè Cova with the circle of poets and painters that had coalesced around Filippo Marinetti's Manifesto of Futurism (1909). In 1914 Sant'Elia exhibited a group of drawings under the title La Città Nuova — The New City — at the Nuove Tendenze show in Milan. The drawings came with a manifesto, published in July 1914 and subsequently appropriated (over Sant'Elia's protest) as the Futurist Manifesto of Architecture.

The drawings describe a city organised around multi-level transport. Skyscrapers rise in vast stepped setbacks, the bases extending outward to meet elevated roadways at upper levels. External elevator shafts run diagonally up the exteriors of the towers. Subterranean railways run beneath the streets. Powerhouses, communications towers, and industrial buildings sit beside apartments and offices without any of the nineteenth-century separation between industrial and residential use. Materials are concrete, iron, glass. The ornament is the structure itself.

The manifesto text is worth quoting in one passage:

We must invent and rebuild the futurist city like an immense and tumultuous shipyard, agile, mobile and dynamic in every detail; and the futurist house must be like a gigantic machine.

Nothing about this in 1914 was buildable at the scale proposed. Reinforced concrete existed, but not the vocabulary of curtain-wall high-rises that would make such a city feasible. The drawings are partly prophecy, partly propaganda.

docs.title: Why it failed
docs.text:
Sant'Elia died in the war. He volunteered for Italian service in 1915, served in the Lombard Volunteer Cyclist Battalion, and was killed in the battle of Monfalcone on 10 October 1916 at the age of twenty-eight. The Città Nuova existed at his death only as a body of drawings and a manifesto; he had built almost nothing. There was no successor to continue the project, though Futurism as a movement absorbed the drawings into its iconography.

A second reason the Città Nuova failed: it was generic. The drawings do not propose building a specific Futurist city on a specific site. They propose that every new building be of this kind. There was no commission to solicit, no client to approach. The proposal was for an entire built environment and could not have been started piecemeal.

docs.title: What-if
docs.text:
Sant'Elia's drawings are the visual template for every stepped, setback skyscraper city of the twentieth century. Hugh Ferriss, in New York in the 1920s, was drawing from the same toolkit (and probably, though Ferriss never acknowledged it, directly from Sant'Elia's plates). The 1916 New York zoning resolution, which mandated setbacks above specified heights, gave American skyscrapers a silhouette that looked remarkably like Sant'Elia's drawings. Gotham City, as envisioned by any comic-book artist or film director working from the 1930s onward, is Sant'Elia with gangsters.

What was never built was the full programme: the combined elevated road, subterranean rail, external elevator, and stepped tower, unified into one continuous infrastructural fabric. Pieces of it exist in Chicago's Wacker Drive, in Tokyo's elevated expressways, in the walkway systems of Hong Kong. Sant'Elia's integrated scheme, where every building participates in the transport network, remains undone. The interesting question is whether the undoneness is a failure or a mercy.

Next: Hotel Attraction →

docs.title: Hotel Attraction
docs.text: ArchitectAntoni Gaudí (1852–1926) Designed1908, in Barcelona, from second-hand descriptions of the New York site Intended siteLower Manhattan, New York Height / scale360 m — considerably taller than anything in New York at the time (the Flatiron was 87 m) Statusunbuilt — commission lapsed, designs largely lost to 1936 fire A cluster of parabolic towers about a taller central one, with the Flatiron for scale

docs.title: What it was
docs.text:
In the summer of 1908 two American investors visited Barcelona to see Antoni Gaudí about a commission. They wanted a hotel on Lower Manhattan that would be the tallest building in the world. They had chosen Gaudí because they had seen his Casa Milà going up, and they believed that a skyscraper in Gaudí's idiom would be the signature object Manhattan lacked.

Gaudí's design, worked out in Barcelona over the following year, was a parabolic tower 360 metres tall — more than four times the height of the Flatiron, and roughly fifty metres taller than the Eiffel Tower. The profile is a bullet: wide at the base, tapering in a continuous parabolic curve to a small rounded tip. Terraces project from the exterior at regular intervals, each cantilevered in Gaudí's signature Art Nouveau vocabulary. At the crown, five star-shaped spires cluster around a central spike, with the whole topped by an enormous observation sphere lit from within at night. The interior programme describes ballrooms, restaurants on every fifth floor, several hundred guest rooms, and an apartment for the owner at the very top.

The drawings were handled by a young architect in Gaudí's studio, Joan Matamala. The final set of plates, watercoloured and exhibited privately, showed the tower silhouetted against a schematic Lower Manhattan skyline. The building was the skyline, because the skyline of 1908 was almost nothing.

docs.title: Why it failed
docs.text:
The investors, Gaudí, and Matamala never met again after 1908. Gaudí's energy was, by that year, almost entirely absorbed by the Sagrada Família — the building that would occupy him until his death in 1926 and continue for a century thereafter. He was not in a position to travel to New York to supervise a project of that scale, and there is no evidence the American financing was ever confirmed. The commission quietly lapsed.

What happened to the drawings is its own melancholy story. A set of plates was held in Gaudí's studio at the Sagrada Família. In July 1936, at the start of the Spanish Civil War, anarchist militias broke into the Sagrada Família workshop and burned most of the contents — Gaudí's plaster models, his notebooks, his plans. The Hotel Attraction drawings were among the materials destroyed. What survives is a small set of Matamala's copies and reconstructions drawn in the 1950s from memory; these are the basis of all subsequent reproductions.

docs.title: What-if
docs.text:
A 360-metre Gaudí tower in 1908 Manhattan would have preceded the Woolworth Building (241 m, 1913), the Chrysler Building (319 m, 1930), and the Empire State Building (381 m, 1931). It would have arrived two decades before the skyscraper boom of the late 1920s, at a moment when the skyscraper typology was still being invented. Had the tower gone up as designed, the Manhattan skyline of the twentieth century would have been organised around a biomorphic Catalan landmark, and the rectilinear skyscraper aesthetic that came to define New York would have had to answer to that prior.

After the September 2001 attacks destroyed the World Trade Center, the Hotel Attraction was briefly revived as a proposal for Ground Zero by a group of Spanish and Catalan designers. The revival had no serious institutional backing and nothing came of it. Gaudí's tower remains where it has always been: on paper, copied from a lost original, imagined against a skyline that never received it.

Next: Chicago Tribune Column →

docs.title: Chicago Tribune Column
docs.text: ArchitectAdolf Loos (1870–1933) Designed1922, submitted to the Chicago Tribune Tower competition Intended siteMichigan Avenue at the river, Chicago Height / scaleApproximately 122 m — a single colossal Doric column on an office plinth Statusunbuilt — competition won by Howells & Hood A plinth, a fluted Doric shaft, and a capital — the column as skyscraper

docs.title: What it was
docs.text:
In 1922 the Chicago Tribune announced a competition to design "the most beautiful office building in the world" — its new headquarters, to be built on Michigan Avenue at the river. The prize was $50,000 and a commission. The competition drew 263 entries from across Europe and America. The winning entry, by John Mead Howells and Raymond Hood, was a Gothic Revival tower with flying buttresses at the crown; it was built, and it stands there today.

Adolf Loos, the Viennese architect who had argued in Ornament and Crime (1910) that ornament was a mark of cultural primitivism, submitted an entry that was itself an enormous ornament. His tower is a single Doric column. The plinth — eleven storeys of offices — is a black granite cube, banded by horizontal string-courses. The shaft of the column rises above the plinth, fluted, in white stone, at twenty-one storeys. The capital is a Doric abacus and echinus, executed at the scale of a three-storey building. There is no entasis; Loos draws the shaft as a pure cylinder.

The total height is approximately 122 metres, which would have made the column the seventh-tallest building in the world at the time. The programme of the building is shoehorned into the cylindrical shaft — elevators at the core, offices pinwheeling around them, the square plan abandoned above the plinth in favour of circular floor plates.

Loos's argument was that a commercial newspaper, which traded in the quotidian, should be housed in a building whose form was the single best-known piece of architectural iconography on the planet. A Doric column says "classical, serious, institutional" without saying a word. The building was, in this sense, the ultimate piece of architectural branding.

docs.title: Why it failed
docs.text:
The jury placed Loos's entry well down the list. It was too literal, too visibly a joke against the competition's own pretensions. The Tribune wanted a monument that said newspaper, not a monument that said look at this paradox about ornament. Loos's entry arrived from Vienna when the winning entries were being reviewed and was recorded as having received no serious consideration by the judges.

The larger reason the column failed is that nobody else wanted one either. In the years after 1922 a number of architects (Loos himself, half-jokingly; a few American architects, rather earnestly) played with the idea of a classical-order skyscraper. The idea never produced a building. By the late 1920s Art Deco had supplied the American skyscraper with its preferred vocabulary — stepped setbacks, ornament integrated with structure — and the free-standing column as a skyscraper became unambiguously historical.

docs.title: What-if
docs.text:
If the column had been built, Chicago would have a piece of architectural thinking at its riverfront that no other American city has. The column would have been seen two ways simultaneously: as a literal monument to Western civilisation, and as Loos's sly demonstration that a single ornament at sufficient scale becomes the building. Contemporary architecture's preoccupation with icons — Frank Gehry's Guggenheim Bilbao, Herzog & de Meuron's stadiums, Norman Foster's Gherkin — is a weaker and later version of the argument Loos was making in one drawing in 1922.

What did get built at the Tribune site is the Gothic Revival tower by Howells and Hood, with flying buttresses modelled on the Butter Tower of Rouen Cathedral. It is a handsome and thoroughly literal building. The other entry that almost won, and almost changed American architecture, was Eliel Saarinen's — a stepped modernist tower whose silhouette went on to shape every skyscraper built in Manhattan during the late 1920s. Saarinen's entry was a phantom twice over: unbuilt, and widely imitated.

docs.title: Cardiff Bay Opera House
docs.text: ArchitectZaha Hadid (1950–2016) Designed1994 — won the Cardiff Bay Opera House Trust international competition, beating 269 entries Intended siteCardiff Bay, Wales — a regeneration zone on the waterfront Height / scale1,900-seat opera house with supporting chamber hall, foyers, and rehearsal rooms; total approximately 25,000 m² Statusunbuilt — Millennium Commission refused Lottery funding Collision of tilted prismatic volumes and a sharply cantilevered fin

docs.title: What it was
docs.text:
In 1994 the Cardiff Bay Opera House Trust ran an international competition for a new opera house on the redeveloped Cardiff waterfront. The project had political weight. Wales had campaigned for its own national opera house for decades; the Millennium Commission — the body distributing UK National Lottery funds for major cultural projects — had indicated it would consider Cardiff Bay Opera as a flagship Millennium project. The competition attracted 269 entries from around the world. The jury, chaired by the Welsh architect Norman Foster's former partner, awarded first prize to Zaha Hadid.

Hadid's scheme is a collision of sharp angular volumes. The main opera hall — a prismatic volume — leans into a second prism containing the chamber hall and the rehearsal rooms. A sharply cantilevered fin projects over the bay. The foyers wrap around the halls at ground level in a series of tilted planes that open toward the water. The whole composition has no right angles on the exterior; every surface is tilted. The building reads, from across the bay, as a crystalline intrusion into the waterfront — something that has just landed there, still settling.

The interior planning solved the opera-house problems soundly: a 1,900-seat main auditorium with a full fly-tower, a 400-seat chamber hall for recitals, rehearsal rooms sized for the Welsh National Opera and the BBC National Orchestra of Wales, and the sequence of foyers, bars, and terraces that a major cultural building needs. Hadid's engineering partners on the scheme were Ove Arup. The project was technically, programmatically, and logistically coherent.

docs.title: Why it failed
docs.text:
The Millennium Commission refused to fund it. The official reason given was that the project was insufficiently commercial — the hall's seat count and programming plan, the Commission held, were not robust enough to pay back the operating subsidy. The unofficial reasons were many: Hadid's design was regarded by some Welsh political figures as too foreign, too radical, insufficiently Welsh; she was a woman; she was Iraqi; she had built almost nothing at the time (the Vitra Fire Station in Germany, 1993, was her first completed building). The tabloid press ran campaigns against the scheme. A competing proposal for a rugby stadium on the site — the Millennium Stadium — was funded instead, and was built.

The rejection was a public and humiliating one for Hadid. She later described it as the worst professional setback of her career. It was also not the only time: in 1996 she won a competition to design the Victoria and Albert Museum Boilerhouse extension in London, and that project also failed to find funding and was abandoned. The Cardiff rejection is emblematic of a specific moment in the mid-1990s in which Hadid's drawings were celebrated in the architectural press but her buildings were not being commissioned. She did not complete a second built building until 1998.

docs.title: What-if
docs.text:
A built Cardiff Bay Opera House would have been one of the first major cultural buildings of the Deconstructivist movement, completed before Gehry's Guggenheim Bilbao (1997). Cardiff, not Bilbao, would have been the first example of the "Bilbao effect" — the regeneration of a declining industrial city by a single spectacular building. The prominence of Hadid as an architect, and the pace of her subsequent commissions, would have accelerated by several years. Her built œuvre — which grew to include the MAXXI in Rome, the Heydar Aliyev Centre in Baku, the London Aquatics Centre, and the Guangzhou Opera House — would have been bracketed on the front end by Cardiff.

What actually happened was almost as influential. Hadid's drawings for the competition, her paintings and her constructions on paper, circulated in the architectural press for years. They taught a generation of architects that competition boards could be as consequential as built buildings. Hadid won Cardiff, lost the funding, and became better known internationally than the winners of many built competitions of the same period. By 2004 she was the first woman to win the Pritzker Prize. By her death in 2016 her practice was global and her built work was everywhere. The Cardiff Opera became, in retrospect, a kind of credential: the building she would have built, had she been allowed to. After its cancellation, the cancellations and near-cancellations of other projects became easier for her, and then easier still for every architect who came after, to resist. The phantom opera house helped train the institutions that later commissioned the built ones.

Next: Crystal Island, Moscow →

docs.title: Crystal Island
docs.text: ArchitectFoster + Partners (Norman Foster), London Designed2007; presented at MIPIM Cannes, March 2008 Intended siteNagatinskaya Poyma, Moscow — a flood plain bend in the Moskva River, south of the city centre Height / scale450 m tall; 2,500,000 m² floor area — the largest single building ever proposed Statusunbuilt — construction halted by 2008 financial crisis, never resumed A tented glass envelope enclosing apartments, offices, schools, and an international school

docs.title: What it was
docs.text:
Crystal Island was commissioned in 2007 by Shalva Chigirinsky, a Russian real-estate developer with close ties to the Moscow city administration. Foster's brief was to design a single building capable of housing a substantial satellite city on a flood-plain site at a bend in the Moskva River, nine kilometres south of central Moscow.

The resulting building is an enormous tented enclosure. A conical envelope of glass and steel rises from a roughly circular base to a single peak 450 metres above ground. Inside the envelope, supported on a secondary structure of trusses and shear walls, rises a conventional city: 900 apartments, 3,000 hotel rooms, 300,000 square metres of commercial and retail space, an international school, a sports centre, a theatre, and fourteen thousand parking spaces. The total enclosed floor area is 2,500,000 square metres — about four times the Pentagon and the largest single building ever seriously proposed. Foster's own studio estimated that the project, if built, would house approximately 30,000 people and employ another 27,000.

The outer envelope does two things. First, it creates a climate-controlled internal city — Moscow's climate is brutal in both directions, and an enclosed building allows a constant interior temperature. Second, it gives the complex a single architectural identity. From across the river it reads as one peak — a Russian Mont Saint-Michel — rather than as a cluster of buildings. The skin is gridded with panels of variable opacity, which can open or close according to the season; in summer the south-facing panels shade the interior, in winter they open to admit solar gain.

docs.title: Why it failed
docs.text:
Groundbreaking on Crystal Island took place in March 2008. Construction began on the foundation pit. Then the global financial crisis arrived in September 2008. Chigirinsky's company, Russian Land, lost access to capital. The Moscow city administration — under Mayor Yuri Luzhkov, who had approved the project — came under political pressure to halt the scheme. Luzhkov was dismissed by Russian President Dmitry Medvedev in 2010 on a corruption investigation. The project's planning permissions were revoked in the aftermath. The site was cleared and left empty; the foundation pit was filled in.

Chigirinsky himself fled Russia in 2009 under threat of prosecution. Russian Land entered insolvency. No successor developer picked up Crystal Island, and by 2015 the proposal was formally dead. The site at Nagatinskaya Poyma remained undeveloped until 2020, when a theme park — "Dream Island," Moscow's largest — opened on approximately the same ground. The new building is a functioning attraction with Disney-styled architecture and a fraction of the floor area Foster had proposed.

docs.title: What-if
docs.text:
A built Crystal Island would have been, by a substantial margin, the largest single building on the planet. It would have tested the question of whether a mixed-use interior city under a single envelope could operate as a coherent community, or would have fragmented into clusters of unrelated uses sharing a skin. The engineering was achievable; Foster had previously built the Millau Viaduct and the Reichstag dome, and his office had developed the expertise to manage the structural and environmental systems at this scale.

What Crystal Island shares with many of the late phantoms in this catalog is a dependence on speculative capital. Tatlin's tower required a revolution; Speer's Volkshalle required a victorious war; Wright's Illinois required a client who never arrived. Crystal Island required the mid-2000s Russian construction boom to continue. When that boom stopped in September 2008, the building stopped with it. The building was feasible; the economic conditions that had made it feasible evaporated, and did not return.

This is the characteristic mode of twenty-first-century phantom architecture. Unlike the earlier phantoms — which failed for political or ideological reasons, or because the material science was not yet available — Crystal Island failed because the money disappeared. The same is true of many other 2000s-era megaprojects: Santiago Calatrava's Chicago Spire (2007, halted 2008), the original Dubai Palm Deira (2002, halted 2008), Rem Koolhaas's RAK Gateway (2008, halted 2010). The financial crisis produced a whole generation of phantoms. Crystal Island is the largest of them.

docs.title: Mega-City Pyramid / TRY 2004
docs.text: ArchitectShimizu Corporation Research and Development Institute Designed1989, as the TRY 2004 concept study Intended siteTokyo Bay — a 12 km × 12 km footprint in the open water Height / scale2,004 m tall (the project name); approximately 750,000 residents; 204 stacked modular cities Statusunbuilt — material science has not yet caught up Tetrahedral truss holding spherical city modules at nodes

docs.title: What it was
docs.text:
In 1989, at the height of Japan's asset-price bubble, Shimizu Corporation — one of Japan's four largest general contractors — published a concept study for the largest man-made structure ever proposed. The project was called TRY 2004, named for its intended height in metres. It is often referred to simply as the Mega-City Pyramid.

The structure is a tetrahedral truss 2,004 metres tall, resting on twelve kilometres of footprint in Tokyo Bay. The truss is not a solid pyramid; it is a spaceframe — a regular lattice of tetrahedral cells, each node reinforced, the whole assembled from carbon-nanotube struts. Inside the lattice, at selected nodes, hang spherical "sky-cities" — each a self-contained residential, commercial, and agricultural community for approximately 3,750 people. Two hundred and four sky-cities hang within the lattice, for a total population of roughly 750,000.

The sky-cities are connected to each other by an internal transport network: high-speed lifts and personal-rapid-transit pods running along the truss members. Each sky-city has its own microclimate; the interior of the lattice has its own weather, managed by the shape of the outer skin. Solar, wave, and wind generation supply power. Fresh water is gathered from rain and condensation on the outer surface. The pyramid was designed, in Shimizu's presentation, as a response to Japan's expected late-twenty-first-century population pressure and the unsuitability of low-lying coastal Japan for denser development in an era of rising seas.

The programme was prepared as a detailed feasibility study. Shimizu's engineers specified structural loads, material requirements, construction sequences, and cost estimates in 1989 yen. The cost was approximately ¥80 trillion, then roughly US $720 billion.

docs.title: Why it failed
docs.text:
The material science does not yet exist. The structural truss required — 2 km high, self-supporting against wind loading, spanning between nodes of several hundred metres — can be analysed in finite-element simulations, and the simulations indicate that no steel or reinforced-concrete construction can do the job. The study's engineers specified carbon-nanotube-reinforced composites as the structural member. Carbon nanotubes were discovered in 1991, two years after the study was published; structural-grade nanotube materials at industrial volumes did not exist then and still do not. Shimizu's scheme was a bet on a material that had not yet been invented.

The economic environment also failed to cooperate. 1989 was the last year of the Japanese asset bubble; by 1991 the bubble had deflated, and Japan entered the two-decade stagnation known as the Lost Decades. Large speculative construction proposals from 1989 Japan — TRY 2004, the X-Seed 4000 tower, the Sky City 1000 — all went onto the shelf. Shimizu has revisited TRY 2004 periodically since, most recently in 2012, but always as a future-possibilities study rather than as an active project.

docs.title: What-if
docs.text:
A built TRY 2004 would solve a specific problem — how to house three-quarters of a million people on effectively no land — that most coastal cities will eventually need to solve. Its engineering would be unprecedented. The carbon-nanotube lattice, if made to work, would be the material breakthrough of the century. The internal organisation of 204 self-contained sky-cities, each with its own microclimate and its own governance, would be an experiment in stacked urbanism at a scale never previously attempted.

The more honest thing to say about the Mega-City Pyramid is that it is a test of what a society will pay for future-proofing. Japan in 1989 was the wealthiest society in history on a per-capita basis, and its largest contractor proposed the pyramid as a plausible sixty-year undertaking. Japan since 1989 has had neither the will nor the material sciences to revisit the plan seriously. If climate-driven coastal pressure continues to accelerate, some coastal city somewhere will eventually be forced to consider pyramid-scale solutions. Whether the structure they build resembles TRY 2004, or something entirely different, is a question whose answer is still being drafted.

For now, the pyramid remains a drawing in Shimizu's research library, annotated with materials specifications for a substance that nature has not yet allowed us to fabricate at scale. It is a phantom of the most precise kind: a building waiting on one specific technological door to open.

docs.title: Broadacre City
docs.text: ArchitectFrank Lloyd Wright (1867–1959) Designed1932, refined continuously until Wright's death; large model built by apprentices at Taliesin, 1934–1935 Intended siteAnywhere with usable land — the scheme is generic and non-geographical Height / scaleOne acre per family; one-mile square neighbourhood units; one vertical spire per district Statusunbuilt — a 4-square-mile model toured the US, 1935 Distributed single-family units on individual acres; one civic spire per district

docs.title: What it was
docs.text:
Broadacre City is Frank Lloyd Wright's answer to Le Corbusier's Plan Voisin, drawn at almost the same time and arguing the exact opposite. Where Le Corbusier wanted to concentrate the population in eighteen towers, Wright wanted to spread it out across the landscape — one acre of land per family, homes arranged not in streets but in large loose lots, connected by a grid of highways that treated the land between homes as productive acreage.

Wright first presented Broadacre in his 1932 book The Disappearing City and elaborated it in a lecture series at Princeton that year. The scheme took physical form in 1934–1935 when Wright's apprentices at Taliesin built a 3.6-metre-square model depicting four square miles of Broadacre at 1:75 scale. The model showed:

  • Single-family Usonian houses, each on an acre of ground, each with a car and a kitchen garden.
  • Light industry distributed among the homes rather than concentrated — factories small enough to be walked to, or driven to in minutes.
  • Civic buildings — schools, libraries, a single tall office tower per administrative district — placed at road junctions.
  • Agricultural land interleaved with residential and industrial. The boundary between "city" and "farm" was deliberately dissolved.
  • A highway grid, a rail line, and aerodromes for the small personal aircraft Wright expected everyone to eventually own.

The model toured the United States in 1935, with stops in Pittsburgh, Washington, and Madison. Wright presented it as a fully-worked planning scheme. The press coverage was respectful. No city adopted it.

docs.title: Why it failed
docs.text:
Broadacre failed because no one ever has the authority to execute it. The scheme required distributing land — one acre per family — across a region of several hundred square miles. That required eminent domain at a scale only a nation-state could exercise, and political will such a state almost never had. Even the Tennessee Valley Authority, the great experiment in regional planning from the same decade, did not reorganise land ownership on a Broadacre basis.

What happened instead was that Broadacre was built without anyone deciding to build it. Post-war American suburbanisation produced, in aggregate, a landscape strongly resembling Wright's scheme: low-density single-family homes on half-acre lots, connected by a highway grid, with industrial and commercial functions distributed among residential neighbourhoods. The outcome differed from Broadacre in two specific ways. First, the landscape was developed privately, piece by piece, rather than as a coordinated plan — so there are fewer of the civic amenities Wright drew (the schools, the arts centres, the libraries) and more of the private amenities the market provided (shopping malls, gas stations). Second, the land grants were nominal: a suburban lot is typically an eighth of an acre, not a full acre, and the productive agriculture Wright envisioned never happened.

docs.title: What-if
docs.text:
A full Broadacre America would have looked like the suburbs we actually got, with additional civic infrastructure and actual agricultural yield from the distributed acreage. It would have required the federal government to act as a planner on a scale it has never acted. The more interesting counterfactual is whether Wright was right about the underlying premise — that the automobile and the telephone made the dense industrial city obsolete, and that America's future belonged to a distributed, small-town, technologically modern rural landscape.

The automobile and the telephone did produce the distributed settlement pattern Wright predicted. What they did not produce was the civic thickness Wright thought would accompany it. A Broadacre township, in Wright's drawings, has a library, a hospital, a school, a philharmonic hall, and a research laboratory, each within a few minutes' drive. A suburb of Atlanta in 2026 has a shopping centre, a megachurch, a Chick-fil-A, and a tenth of each of the institutions Wright drew. The geography came true. The culture did not. Broadacre remains phantom even where, geographically, it was executed.

Next: The Illinois / Mile-High →

docs.title: The Illinois / Mile-High
docs.text: ArchitectFrank Lloyd Wright (1867–1959) Designed1956, presented 16 October 1956 at the Sherman Hotel, Chicago Intended siteChicago lakefront, unspecified lot Height / scale1,609 m (one mile); 528 storeys; 100,000 occupants; atomic-powered elevators Statusunbuilt — Wright was 89; no client; no commission A tripod-braced needle rising from a cluster of conventional skyscrapers

docs.title: What it was
docs.text:
On 16 October 1956, Frank Lloyd Wright — then 89 years old — unveiled at a Chicago press conference a project for a 1,609-metre skyscraper. He called it The Illinois. The press and subsequent history have mostly called it Mile-High.

The building is a single triangular needle, tapering continuously from a base of approximately 120 metres to a slim tip at the summit. The tripod base is braced by three massive legs, which Wright intended to be executed in steel and reinforced concrete. The interior was to be organised as 528 storeys. Lifts — atomic-powered, according to Wright's announcement, though no such lift had ever been engineered — would run at speeds of up to sixty miles per hour in "quintuple-deck" banks. The building would hold 100,000 occupants and 15,000 parked cars, with helicopter landings at the upper levels.

Wright's schematic rendering, prepared with his office, shows the Illinois rising from a cluster of Chicago skyscrapers — the Palmolive Building, the Wrigley, the Tribune Tower, the Merchandise Mart — each rendered at approximately one-tenth of the Illinois's height. The drawing makes clear what the tower is for: it is a dare. It says that the Chicago skyline of 1956, tall as it is, is provincial; that a real skyscraper should dwarf everything around it; and that it is possible, with enough will, to build such a thing now.

Wright had no client. He announced the project without a commission, without a site, and without a declared source of financing. The press release was the project.

docs.title: Why it failed
docs.text:
No one commissioned it, no one funded it, and Wright died two and a half years after the announcement, on 9 April 1959, without the project having progressed beyond its initial drawings. There is no evidence he expected the Illinois to be built. The announcement was a provocation, a statement of principle, a demonstration that the skyscraper could be taken further than anyone had taken it.

Several specific objections made it infeasible in 1956. The tripod base's lateral bracing was possible but expensive. Lift technology in 1956 topped out at speeds that would have made the upper 400 storeys of the building functionally unreachable — a trip to the top would have taken well over an hour, during which time the elevator would have been the tallest structure actively in use. The "atomic-powered" lifts Wright mentioned were fictional; no atomic elevator system has ever been built. The wind loading at a mile of altitude would have required a base foundation of unprecedented size and depth.

Modern engineering — post-2010 — can build a mile-high building. The Jeddah Tower, under intermittent construction in Saudi Arabia since 2013, is designed to exceed a kilometre and has targeted a mile. The engineering problems Wright waved at are solvable. The economic question — whether there is enough demand for office space at a mile in altitude to pay back the construction — is a separate question, and it has not yet been answered with a completed building anywhere on earth.

docs.title: What-if
docs.text:
Had the Illinois been built, Chicago's skyline would have had a single landmark dominating every other building by a factor of four. The Willis Tower (1974, 442 m), itself briefly the world's tallest, would have been a short afterthought. The architectural conversation of the late twentieth century — whether the skyscraper could continue rising, whether the tall building had a natural limit — would have been a different conversation, because Wright would have resolved it with a built example.

The more interesting thing Wright did with the Illinois was to demonstrate that a single building could, as an object, be a complete statement about what was possible. The Illinois is what a late-career Wright considered his summation: not a house, not a museum, not a church, but a tower so tall that it became a question mark over the idea of cities. Every subsequent architect designing an ultra-tall tower — Foster's Millennium Tower in Tokyo, Koolhaas's unbuilt plans for Jakarta, the Kingdom Tower and its successors — has been answering Wright's question. The Illinois taught the discipline to think at mile-scale. It did this without ever leaving the page.

Next: Palace of the Soviets →

docs.title: Plan Voisin
docs.text: ArchitectLe Corbusier (Charles-Édouard Jeanneret, 1887–1965) Designed1925, presented at the Exposition internationale des Arts Décoratifs, Paris Intended siteThree square kilometres of central Paris, north of the Seine, between the Gare de l'Est and the Louvre Height / scaleEighteen identical 200-metre cruciform-plan towers, spaced 400 m apart, on a uniform orthogonal grid of elevated highways Statusunbuilt — proposal rejected by municipal authorities Three of the eighteen cruciform towers at their true spacing, with Notre-Dame and the Eiffel Tower for scale; the full grid in the key plan

docs.title: What it was
docs.text:
Plan Voisin was Le Corbusier's proposal to demolish three square kilometres of central Paris — the Marais, parts of the 1st, 3rd, and 4th arrondissements, the streets around the Rue de Rivoli north of the Louvre — and replace them with eighteen identical 200-metre skyscrapers on a regular grid of elevated highways. The scheme was named for Voisin, the aviation and automobile manufacturer that had funded its publication at the 1925 Paris decorative-arts exposition. Voisin's money bought the pavilion in which the plan was displayed.

The towers are cruciform in plan — a plus-sign footprint — spaced 400 metres apart on an orthogonal grid. Between the towers, the ground is a park. Above the park, at the second-storey level, runs a grid of elevated highways with pedestrian decks below and vehicle traffic above. Most of historic central Paris is gone. The Louvre, the Tuileries, the Place Vendôme, the Palais Royal, and a handful of other designated historic buildings remain — preserved as monuments in what is otherwise a tabula rasa.

Le Corbusier described the scheme in Urbanisme (1925) with the specific conviction that the historic Paris was unworkable: its streets too narrow for motor traffic, its buildings too dark and crowded, its populations too concentrated at street level. The answer was to move the population up into towers with light, air, and park views; to move the traffic onto elevated corridors; and to free the ground level for parkland.

The plan was exhibited as a large model and as a set of axonometric drawings. The model showed the eighteen towers in precise regularity, each identical, standing over a park crossed by straight highways.

docs.title: Why it failed
docs.text:
Paris refused. Le Corbusier's proposal received public attention and some sympathetic reviews, but no municipal authority seriously entertained demolishing the Marais. The combined cost, displacement, and cultural objection was prohibitive. By the mid-1930s Le Corbusier himself had moderated the scheme in favour of more incremental planning proposals (the Ville Radieuse, 1930, applied similar principles to less historically sensitive sites).

What the plan did was educate an entire generation of urbanists in the doctrine of the tower-in-the-park. Housing projects across Europe and America built between 1945 and 1975 — London's Trellick Tower, Paris's own post-war social housing estates, New York's Stuyvesant Town, Chicago's Cabrini-Green, the Pruitt-Igoe estate in St Louis — implemented pieces of Le Corbusier's prescription on cleared or new ground. The social outcomes were mixed. Pruitt-Igoe was demolished in 1972; Cabrini-Green followed. The tower-in-the-park typology, applied in full, produced environments that the residents reliably abandoned when they had the means to.

docs.title: What-if
docs.text:
If Paris had accepted Plan Voisin, the Marais would be gone. So would the Palais Royal, the narrow streets behind Les Halles, the bookshop-studded alleys around the Place des Vosges. Eighteen identical skyscrapers would stand over a cleared landscape, visible from every point in Paris and almost indistinguishable from each other. The tourist trade that sustains Paris's economy would have developed around different artefacts — the preserved Louvre and Notre Dame — while the city's fine grain would have been replaced by a geometry best appreciated from the air.

What actually happened was that Paris preserved itself with particular ferocity. The Malraux Law of 1962 established protected sectors for historic quarters; the Marais is one of them. The city built its Plan-Voisin-scale tower concentration not at the centre, but at La Défense, five kilometres west of the Louvre, outside the Boulevard Périphérique and out of sight of anyone standing on the Champs-Élysées. Le Corbusier's towers did arrive in Paris, but as Paris's suburbs rather than its centre. That is the version of the plan that survived: towers at the edge, preserved historic core at the middle. It is a compromise the city is now, after fifty years, mostly comfortable with.

docs.title: Palace of the Soviets
docs.text: ArchitectBoris Iofan (1891–1976), with Vladimir Shchuko and Vladimir Gelfreikh Designed1933 (competition); final scheme approved 1934; construction begun 1937 Intended siteVolkhonka Street, Moscow — the site cleared by the 1931 demolition of the Cathedral of Christ the Saviour Height / scale415 m total, including a 100 m statue of Lenin; 100,000 m² main hall; stepped tiered base Statuspartially built — foundations; steel frame to 7 storeys; dismantled for war effort 1941–42 Tiered stepped base with a colossal Lenin at the summit — a finger of granite, raised

docs.title: What it was
docs.text:
The Palace of the Soviets was to be the central building of the Soviet Union — its parliament, its principal assembly hall, its ceremonial space. The original competition was announced in 1931 and drew entries from around the world, including Le Corbusier (whose entry, a modernist scheme with vast parabolic vaults, reached the final round and was rejected). In 1933 a committee settled on Boris Iofan's scheme, which was reworked through several iterations until 1934, when the final form was approved.

The final scheme is a tiered stepped base — seven concentric tiers, each smaller than the one below, ascending through 300 metres — topped by a 100-metre-tall statue of Lenin. The total height is 415 metres. Lenin stands with one arm raised, roughly over the site where the cathedral used to be; his index finger alone is to be longer than a bus. The building is sited on a cleared square along Volkhonka Street, a few blocks from the Kremlin, on land previously occupied by the Cathedral of Christ the Saviour. Stalin ordered the cathedral dynamited in December 1931 to clear the site.

Internally, the Palace was to contain a Great Hall seating 21,000 for congresses of the Communist Party; a Lesser Hall seating 6,000; libraries; exhibition spaces; a monumental staircase; and the offices of the Supreme Soviet. The architecture is a heavy stripped classicism, columns and pilasters rendered at enormous scale without ornament, more sculptural than tectonic. The whole tiered volume is the base for the statue.

docs.title: Why it failed
docs.text:
Construction began in 1937. Foundations were excavated — a ring of concrete 140 metres in diameter, sunk into Moscow's waterlogged soil. Steel was fabricated and the lower frame of the stepped base was erected to a height of approximately seven storeys. Photographs from 1938 and 1939 show a ring of black steel rising over the Moscow river.

Then the war came. In 1941, with the German army advancing on Moscow, Soviet engineers dismantled the steel frame of the Palace and used the material for anti-tank defences and for the wartime reconstruction of bridges and rail lines. What remained was the foundation — a submerged concrete ring. The construction never resumed.

After the war, Stalin's architectural priorities shifted. The Seven Sisters (Moscow's seven Stalinist skyscrapers, built 1947–1953) satisfied the regime's need for monumental high-rises without the burden of the Lenin statue or the 415-metre total height. The Palace site sat as an abandoned foundation into the 1950s. In 1958 Khrushchev authorised its conversion into an open-air heated swimming pool — the Moskva Pool — which operated on the foundations until 1994. After the fall of the USSR, the cathedral that had stood on the site before 1931 was rebuilt to the original plans; it was consecrated in 2000 and stands there now.

docs.title: What-if
docs.text:
A completed Palace of the Soviets would have been the tallest building in the world upon completion, and would have held the record until the World Trade Center (1972). It would have set the model for every totalitarian-monument tower of the twentieth century: the plinth-as-base, the figure-as-apex, the architecture as a pedestal for ideology. Some of that model was built anyway — Speer's Volkshalle was designed in the same years, and Iofan's influence on Axis monumental architecture is documented. But the specific image of Lenin-as-skyscraper would have dominated Moscow's skyline in a way no other single image would have.

The site's history is its own strange phantom chain. Cathedral — dynamited. Palace — foundations only, then swimming pool. Pool — drained, demolished. Cathedral — rebuilt to the 1883 drawings. The current building is the 1883 cathedral executed in 1996–2000, occupying the space that was cleared for Iofan in 1931. The Palace of the Soviets is the void around which all the other buildings have circulated.

docs.title: Volkshalle, Germania
docs.text: ArchitectAlbert Speer (1905–1981), to Adolf Hitler's specifications Designed1937–1940; site preparation begun 1939, construction paused indefinitely 1943 Intended siteNorth end of the Great Axis, Welthauptstadt Germania (the planned redevelopment of Berlin) Height / scale290 m total; 250 m internal dome diameter; capacity 180,000 standing Statusunbuilt — regime destroyed before foundations could be laid A drum of columns beneath a 250-metre interior dome — the largest enclosed space ever proposed

docs.title: What it was
docs.text:
Hitler's plan for post-war Berlin, formalised after 1937, was to transform the city into "Welthauptstadt Germania" — the World Capital Germania. The plan was drawn by Albert Speer at Hitler's direct instruction. Its centrepiece was a vast north-south boulevard, seven kilometres long, running from a new southern rail terminal to a new northern government quarter. At the north end of this axis, facing the Reichstag (which was to be retained as a library), would stand the Volkshalle — the People's Hall.

The Volkshalle is a domed assembly building. The drum supporting the dome is 290 metres tall and 320 metres in diameter. Around the drum runs a colonnade of sixteen stone columns, each approximately 70 metres tall. The dome itself has an internal diameter of 250 metres — larger than St Peter's (42 m), larger than the Pantheon (44 m), larger than any enclosed space built or proposed in human history. A small oculus at the crown admits light. The interior is a single volume of 21 million cubic metres, intended to hold 180,000 standing spectators for Party rallies addressed by Hitler from a central speaker's platform.

The building is clad in granite quarried from concentration-camp labour in Mauthausen and Flossenbürg. Speer's drawings are explicit about the intended atmosphere: the dome should be so tall that the upper portion is perpetually lost in mist formed by the breath of the assembled crowd. Hitler wanted the Volkshalle to dwarf every earlier monument — the Pantheon, St Peter's, the US Capitol — by the simple expedient of being larger. It is a phantom built to assert through size alone the legitimacy of a regime.

Site preparation for the axis began in 1939. Streets were widened, buildings demolished, a vast swampy marsh at the Volkshalle's proposed site was tested for load-bearing. The column for the Volkshalle's test footing — the Schwerbelastungskörper, a massive cylindrical concrete block — was cast in 1941 to calibrate the sinking of the Berlin subsoil. It still stands in the Tempelhof district.

docs.title: Why it failed
docs.text:
Germany lost the war. Speer's designs for Germania — including the Volkshalle, the triumphal arch, and the Great Hall — depended on victory in 1940 or soon after. When the war continued, resources were redirected. Construction on Germania was paused in 1943 and never resumed. Speer himself was imprisoned at Nuremberg from 1946 to 1966. By 1945 Berlin was a ruin; by 1947 the city was divided; by 1961 the wall ran through what would have been Speer's southern rail terminal.

There was also a structural objection to the Volkshalle that Speer himself quietly recognised. A 250-metre unsupported dome is on the edge of what reinforced concrete could achieve in 1940 — perhaps possible, perhaps not. The test footing was cast precisely because Speer's engineers were unsure the Berlin soil could carry the load. The answer, when the footing was measured in the 1940s, was that the soil could not. The Volkshalle's dome was at the limit of the materials and the foundations that existed to support it.

docs.title: What-if
docs.text:
A completed Volkshalle would have been the signature building of a victorious Third Reich. It would have stood for as long as the regime stood, which in the best case for Hitler was probably a few decades. In the actual case, the regime ended in 1945, so the Volkshalle's tenure would have been short. What would have persisted is the precedent: a building whose function was explicitly to be large, to impress by scale alone, to reduce the individual citizen to a standing figure of insignificance beneath an engineered sky.

That precedent persists anyway. The North Korean Ryugyong Hotel (330 m, construction halted 1992) is a descendant. So is the Palace of the Parliament in Bucharest (completed 1997), the second-largest administrative building in the world, commissioned by Ceaușescu in the same spirit. The architecture of authoritarianism has a remarkably consistent palette: granite cladding, stripped classicism, interior spaces at superhuman scale. The Volkshalle was not built, but its syntax was exported — and built.

The granite that was quarried for the Volkshalle survives. Some of it was used after the war for Soviet war memorials in East Berlin, including the Treptower Park memorial. Hitler's granite became, by war's accident, the monument to the soldiers who brought the regime down. The stones outlasted the building that was going to be made of them.

docs.title: The Metropolis of Tomorrow
docs.text: ArchitectHugh Ferriss (1889–1962) Drawn1922–1929, published 1929 as *The Metropolis of Tomorrow* Intended siteA generic American city — no named location Height / scaleTowers rendered at heights of 300–1,000 m; the book's "Business Zone" tower stands to 1,000 feet (approximately 305 m) Statusunbuilt — the drawings are the city Stepped setback skyscrapers rendered at colossal scale

docs.title: What it was
docs.text:
Hugh Ferriss was not, strictly, an architect. He was a renderer — the man whom New York architects of the 1920s hired to produce the charcoal perspective drawings that sold their buildings to clients and to the public. He drew the Shelton Hotel, the Barclay-Vesey Telephone Building, the RCA Building. He drew in charcoal on brown paper, in the low-contrast style that saw a skyscraper as a mountain rising out of permanent dusk. The style became definitive of American cities in the 1920s.

In 1929, at the height of his career, Ferriss published The Metropolis of Tomorrow — a book of his own imagined drawings. The book has three parts. The first reprints his technical drawings for the 1916 New York Zoning Resolution, which established the mandatory setback envelope that shaped every American skyscraper for the next fifty years. The second shows the architects' own drawings for specific Manhattan buildings, reproduced in Ferriss's charcoal technique. The third is Ferriss's own vision: "An Imaginary Metropolis."

The imaginary city is organised by zones. A Business Zone occupies the centre: vast stepped towers, each essentially the 1916 Zoning envelope taken to its maximum, crowded together without streets visible between them, their setbacks cut at different heights so that the city above street level looks like a mountain range. An Art Zone contains philharmonic halls, libraries, a planetarium — rendered as lower, broader buildings with ceremonial approaches. A Science Zone has laboratories resembling cathedrals. Between the zones, elevated roadways on pylons carry traffic at the mid-heights of the buildings, connecting at specific junctions. Aircraft land on the roofs.

Ferriss's drawings are rendered. They are not technical plans. They are composed like landscape paintings, in chiaroscuro, with the details softened by atmosphere. The effect is to present the city as something one cannot quite see — too big, too hazy, too mountainous to be grasped whole.

docs.title: Why it failed
docs.text:
It was never submitted anywhere. Ferriss's drawings were an author's project, published as a book, priced at $7.50 in 1929. The book sold, was widely reviewed, and went into a second printing. It never proposed that any specific city be built according to the drawings. There was no client, no commission, no legal vehicle. The Metropolis of Tomorrow was speculative architecture in the strict sense: it was a book.

What happened instead was imitation. Every film director, comic-book artist, and advertising illustrator who needed to render "the city of the future" between 1929 and 1960 drew from Ferriss. The opening sequences of King Kong, Metropolis (in its American publicity), Things to Come, and Batman: The Animated Series all descend from the book. The charcoal-mountain aesthetic — the setback tower rising out of cloud — became the default visual language of the future. Fifty years later, Ferriss's silhouettes are the first thing a concept artist draws when asked to sketch an American metropolis.

docs.title: What-if
docs.text:
Had American cities been built to Ferriss's plates — had any specific city adopted the three-zone scheme with elevated roadways — the result would have been a more extreme version of what Chicago and Manhattan became anyway. The 1916 zoning setbacks gave American skyscrapers their stepped silhouette; Ferriss's drawings pushed that silhouette to its maximum. A Ferrissian Manhattan would have had taller, more widely-spaced towers, connected by mid-air roads, and with most of the ground level abandoned to service traffic. Something like that was built, in pieces, across the American megacities of the twentieth century. It is what every highway-borne approach to downtown Chicago, Dallas, or Los Angeles is trying to be.

The more interesting thing Ferriss produced is the aesthetic. The drawings proved that the rendering could be the work. For a phantom building, the drawing is not a sketch for something else — it is the whole output. Every competition board produced in the decades since has been trying to achieve what Ferriss did in The Metropolis of Tomorrow: to make a drawing that is more persuasive than any photograph of a real building would be.
