docs.title: Monument to the Third International
docs.text: ArchitectVladimir Tatlin (1885–1953) Designed1919–1920; wooden model exhibited in Petrograd, December 1920 Intended sitePetrograd (Leningrad) Height / scale400 m (proposed); would have been the tallest structure in the world, taller than the Eiffel Tower Statusunbuilt — three interior volumes each intended to rotate at its own period A leaning double helix enclosing three rotating volumes — cube, pyramid, cylinder

docs.title: What it was
docs.text:
In 1919 the Department of Fine Arts of the People's Commissariat for Enlightenment commissioned Vladimir Tatlin to design a monument to the Third International — the Comintern, the new coordinating body for world communist parties, founded earlier that year. Tatlin was given no site, no budget, and no engineering staff. He was given the subject.

His design, worked up in his Petrograd studio over 1919 and 1920, is unlike any building before or since. Two interlocking helical steel frameworks, leaning at sixty degrees, twist upward around a common axis. Inside the lattice hang three enclosed volumes in primary geometries: at the bottom, a cube; in the middle, a pyramid; at the top, a cylinder. Above the cylinder, Tatlin added a hemisphere — the "radio station" — from which, in the drawings, broadcast waves radiate.

The three volumes were to rotate. The cube, which housed the legislative assembly of the Comintern, turned once a year. The pyramid, which housed the executive committee, turned once a month. The cylinder, which housed the information bureau and propaganda organs, turned once a day. The hemisphere at the top, which broadcast news across the world, turned once an hour. The entire building was a functioning clock — a building whose structure embodied the periodicity of its institutions.

Tatlin's wooden model, built at a 1:25 scale by his students, was exhibited in Petrograd in December 1920. Lunacharsky, the People's Commissar for Enlightenment, came to see it. Photographs of the model circulated internationally — in Germany, in France, in New York — through the early 1920s.

docs.title: Why it failed
docs.text:
The Soviet Union in 1920 could not build a 400-metre steel tower. The civil war had destroyed much of Russian industry; steel was scarce; engineers with high-rise experience did not exist in the new state; and the country was not in a position to pay for such a project even when it recovered. By 1924 Lenin was dead, and the official Soviet taste — soon to be imposed as doctrine — had shifted away from Constructivist experiment toward the neoclassical socialist realism that produced the Palace of the Soviets a decade later. Tatlin was increasingly out of step. He spent the 1930s working on a glider, Letatlin, trying to give the common man the power of flight. He died in Moscow in 1953, largely forgotten; his rehabilitation into the Soviet canon came only during the Khrushchev thaw.

There is a second question about the design itself: whether the rotating volumes could have been engineered. A cube with an annual rotation rate is trivially possible; a pyramid with a monthly rotation rate is trivially possible; what is harder is structure. The leaning double-helix framework would have required steel fabrication at tolerances the USSR of 1920 had no way of achieving. A full-size version attempted today with modern engineering would be expensive but possible. A full-size version in 1920 Petrograd was technically out of reach.

docs.title: What-if
docs.text:
Tatlin's tower is the most influential unbuilt building of the twentieth century. Every later architect who has designed a monument that moved — that rotated, that shifted, that played a mechanical role as well as a symbolic one — is descended from it. Every architect who has made the structural exoskeleton into the primary figure of a building — from Buckminster Fuller through Richard Rogers to Santiago Calatrava — is descended from it. The tower did more work as a drawing, and as a photograph of a model, than most built buildings do in a century.

The plate of the leaning double helix, published and republished, became a visual shorthand for the entire early Soviet experiment. After 1989, when Communism ended and its architecture was left either demolished or stranded, Tatlin's tower remained — now free of its ideological origins, pure form again. A replica was finally built, at 1:20 scale, for the 2011 Royal Academy exhibition Building the Revolution. It stood in the courtyard of Burlington House for three months. It was the first time Tatlin's tower had been in the same city as a London audience. It was ten metres tall. It was the wrong size. It was the right shape.

docs.title: Continuous Monument
docs.text: ArchitectSuperstudio (Adolfo Natalini, Cristiano Toraldo di Francia, and collaborators), Florence Drawn1969–1971, published as a series of photomontages and texts Intended siteSuperstudio's drawings place the monument across New York, the Alps, the Sahara, the Grand Canyon, Mont Blanc, and much of the rest of the world Height / scaleA single gridded bar of approximately 200 m height, extending indefinitely Statusunbuilt — explicitly a critique A gridded monolithic bar in perspective, running past the edge of the drawing

docs.title: What it was
docs.text:
In 1969 the Florentine architectural collective Superstudio began producing a series of photomontages under the title Il Monumento Continuo. The montages show a featureless gridded bar — approximately 200 metres tall, its surface a uniform lattice of identical square panels — extending across the landscapes of the world. In one montage it rides along the skyline of Manhattan, eclipsing the existing skyscrapers. In another it crosses the Arizona desert, rising out of the sand. In another it cuts across the Alps like a geological rift. In another it runs through the Grand Canyon. In another it loops the planet, and the montage shows it from orbit.

Superstudio produced the drawings as part of their larger project of "critical architecture" — architecture conceived as commentary rather than as commission. The Continuous Monument was not a proposal. It was an image: a demonstration of what an architecture of total homogeneity would look like, applied to the whole planet, and a dare to the reader to find something to object to in it.

The dare is sophisticated. Each element of the Continuous Monument is, individually, unobjectionable. The grid is regular. The proportions are harmonious. The material is presumably durable. The scale is ambitious but not preposterous. What becomes horrifying is the cumulative effect: the whole landscape subsumed by a single architectural language, the whole planet reshaped to a single building. The monument is not any specific tyranny. It is the tyranny of applied reason when reason is insufficiently humble about what it does not know.

Superstudio's text accompanying the montages was explicit:

The history of design has always been the history of tyranny. Now we propose its final triumph: the tyranny that no longer needs a tyrant.

docs.title: Why it failed
docs.text:
The Continuous Monument was never meant to be built. It was meant to be absorbed as an image. Superstudio's work participates in a specific late-1960s moment — the same moment that produced the Situationist détournement, Italian arte povera, and the student protests of 1968 — in which critique through fiction was valued over proposal through design. The Continuous Monument is a photomontage, a piece of visual polemic, an argument against modernism conducted in the visual language of modernism.

Could it have been built? At 200 metres tall, extending indefinitely, the Monument would require engineering and materials at planetary scale. The dimensioning is deliberately at the boundary of the impossible — large enough that the viewer can see how it would look, impossible enough that the viewer knows the image is not a proposal. Had Superstudio drawn something smaller, it would have read as feasible and been engaged as an engineering problem; at the scale they chose, the image reads as an argument.

docs.title: What-if
docs.text:
The Continuous Monument is the closing argument of modernism's universal project. Every modernist proposal before it — Plan Voisin, Broadacre, Tatlin, even Ferriss — had assumed that a single architectural language, applied to the world, would be desirable. Superstudio took the hypothesis seriously and followed it to its conclusion. The conclusion was: it would look like this, and it would be terrifying.

After the Continuous Monument, modernism could no longer assert its universality innocently. The next architectural generation — postmodernism, the contextualism of Colin Rowe, the regionalist turn in the late 1970s — defined itself partly against what Superstudio had shown. If modernism's premise really was a global grid, then architects had to choose: either commit to the grid with open eyes, or step back from the premise. Most architects chose the second. Critical regionalism, which became the dominant international discourse of the 1980s, is Superstudio's argument received.

The specific visual influence is diffuse. Every dystopian megastructure in cinema, from Logan's Run to Blade Runner to Dune, carries something of the Continuous Monument. So do the actual megastructures that have been built: the Shanghai World Financial Center, Dubai's linear developments, the Three Gorges Dam. None of these is the Continuous Monument, but each of them has a Continuous Monument inside it. What Superstudio did was provide the argument that makes those buildings legible as a single species.

docs.title: Dome over Manhattan
docs.text: ArchitectR. Buckminster Fuller (1895–1983), with Shoji Sadao Proposed1960, as a feasibility study and published advocacy piece Intended siteMidtown Manhattan, centred roughly on the Empire State Building Height / scaleApproximately 3 km diameter; 1.6 km high at apex; geodesic aluminium frame Statusunbuilt — speculative A geodesic hemispherical shell over a section of Midtown

docs.title: What it was
docs.text:
Buckminster Fuller's Dome over Manhattan was a proposal to enclose a two-mile-diameter section of Midtown — from roughly 22nd Street to 65th Street, from the East River to the Hudson — under a single geodesic dome approximately 3,000 metres across and 1,600 metres tall at the crown. Inside the dome, the city would continue to function as usual: the Empire State Building, Grand Central, Rockefeller Center, Times Square — all of it would remain, and all of it would be under glass.

The proposition was a thought experiment about energy. Fuller had been developing geodesic domes through the 1950s — the Montreal Biosphere (1967) would be a late realised example — and he had been calculating energy balances for enclosed environments. His argument for Manhattan was that the energy cost of heating and cooling the buildings in the covered area, across a sufficient number of winters, would exceed the energy cost of a single geodesic enclosure that kept the interior at a constant temperature. The dome paid back its construction cost in fuel savings within twenty years. After twenty years, the dome was making money.

Fuller's drawing, produced with his partner Shoji Sadao, shows the dome as a geodesic lattice of thin aluminium struts, glazed with clear panels, sitting over the existing skyline. The skyline would be unchanged; only the weather would be different. Snow would not fall inside; rain would not fall; the temperature would be at 20° Celsius year round.

docs.title: Why it failed
docs.text:
The dome was never proposed to a specific client. Fuller published it as part of his advocacy for geodesic structures and as a way of dramatising the energy argument. No municipal body, private consortium, or federal agency ever received a serious proposal to build it. The capital cost — estimated by Fuller at around $200 million in 1960 dollars, probably an order of magnitude too low — would have required a political and financial coalition that no one assembled.

The structural engineering, by Fuller's lights, was within reach. A 3-kilometre geodesic dome is larger than any geodesic that has been built, but the principle scales: as the sphere grows, the ratio of surface weight to enclosed volume decreases, so a large geodesic is relatively lighter per unit volume than a small one. Fuller's claim — that the dome would be "lighter than the air it contained" — was at least dimensionally plausible.

What would have prevented the dome in practice was the specific question of how the boundary works. What happens at street level where the dome meets Manhattan? How do ships reach the riverside piers? How does the subway vent? How do aircraft overfly the city? These questions had answers in principle — airlock entrances, vented louvres, overflight corridors — but each answer was its own project. The simplicity of Fuller's drawing concealed the programmatic complexity of making the dome actually land on a functioning city.

docs.title: What-if
docs.text:
A domed Manhattan would have been, by some distance, the largest enclosed environment in human history. It would have consumed enormous resources to build. It would also have produced a Manhattan that was effectively weatherless, which would have changed the character of the city in ways Fuller did not entirely anticipate. The snow that whitens Fifth Avenue; the rain that cleans the streets; the sunset that reddens the East Side at the end of summer — all of those phenomena would be outside, and the city inside would be under perpetually flat light.

The dome-over-a-city idea has been rebuilt in small form many times. The Mall of America is effectively a micro-dome. Eden Project in Cornwall is a medium-dome habitat. The covered mall, the covered office atrium, the enclosed arena — all are partial Fullerian answers to the energy argument. What has never been attempted is the full-city version, and given the scale of modern climate control, it is unlikely ever to be attempted in the form Fuller drew.

Fuller's drawing is, like Ferriss's charcoals, more useful as a piece of argumentation than it would have been as a building. It asks the viewer to compute, in their head, the energy budget of heating ten thousand separate buildings versus one very large one. Every time somebody makes that comparison, the dome has done its work.

docs.title: Fun Palace
docs.text: ArchitectCedric Price (1934–2003), with theatre director Joan Littlewood; cybernetics by Gordon Pask Designed1961–1965; site secured at Lea Valley; planning permission refused 1966 Intended siteMill Meads, Stratford, East London (the site that later became the Olympic Park) Height / scaleApproximately 200 m × 80 m frame; 15-storey tall; programme fitted within by crane-moved modules Statusunbuilt — planning permission denied, 1966 A fixed steel gantry with movable activity modules suspended and cranes above

docs.title: What it was
docs.text:
The Fun Palace began as a conversation between the theatre director Joan Littlewood and the young architect Cedric Price in 1961. Littlewood had been running the Theatre Royal Stratford East, staging experimental working-class theatre, and wanted something that could extend what theatre did — a building where audiences were not audiences but participants, where programmes were not scheduled weeks in advance but reconfigured within the week or within the day, where learning, play, and performance happened side by side.

Price's architectural answer was a fixed steel gantry approximately 200 metres long, 80 metres wide, and fifteen storeys tall. The gantry itself was permanent. Everything inside was movable. Rooms, stages, workshops, classrooms, cinemas, and cafes were built as prefabricated modules. Gantry cranes running along the top of the frame moved modules into place, removed them, reconfigured them. A theatre that operated yesterday as a 500-seat proscenium might be reconfigured overnight into three separate workshops, a café, and a film studio.

The building's programme was to be decided partly by its users. Price worked with the cybernetician Gordon Pask on a system of feedback mechanisms — surveys, sensors, user requests — that would inform the weekly crane schedule. The building would, in principle, learn what it wanted to be, and rearrange itself accordingly.

The site was Mill Meads, a post-industrial tract in the Lea Valley, East London. Littlewood and Price secured preliminary financing from a group of private backers and from the London County Council, and planning permission was sought from the West Ham council in whose jurisdiction the site lay. The application was made in 1964.

docs.title: Why it failed
docs.text:
The planning permission was refused in 1966. The stated reasons were a combination of technical objections — the gantry structure was unprecedented, the fire-safety implications of movable partitions were unclear, the likely noise impact on adjacent residential areas was a concern — and political ones. West Ham's council was uneasy about a large, visibly experimental, uncontrolled building arriving in their borough. Littlewood's reputation as a left-wing theatre director did not help. The permission was refused; Price appealed; the appeal failed. By 1967 the project was formally dead.

The more interesting reason the Fun Palace failed is that the specific kind of institution Price and Littlewood imagined — a genuinely user-directed cultural space, operating without a programme fixed by experts — is difficult to establish under any planning regime. Every regulatory body prefers a building to declare what it is going to be. The Fun Palace's core premise was that it was going to be whatever its users, at the moment of their arrival, decided it should be. That answer does not satisfy a planning application.

docs.title: What-if
docs.text:
The Fun Palace's technical and programmatic ideas were absorbed piecemeal over the following decades. The Centre Pompidou in Paris (Rogers and Piano, 1977) is a direct descendant — a flexible shed with services on the exterior, programme in the interior, and a reconfigurability that Price's project had prototyped on paper. The Venice Biennale pavilions, the Serpentine Gallery's annual temporary structure, the MIT Media Lab, and the Dutch "crystal palace" cultural centres of the 1980s are all Fun Palace descendants.

What none of these buildings have is the cybernetic user-participation element. The Pompidou presents exhibitions curated by expert curators; the programme shifts slowly, through institutional deliberation, not responsively. The Fun Palace's claim — that the building itself should be a learning system, reshaping itself on a weekly rhythm — has never been tested at scale. Every time somebody proposes a "smart building" or a "responsive architecture," they are proposing a fragment of what Price and Littlewood imagined sixty-five years ago. The fragment usually gets built. The whole does not.

The Mill Meads site, rejected for the Fun Palace in 1966, was eventually chosen as the heart of the London 2012 Olympic Park. The venue Price imagined did not get built there; the Aquatics Centre, the velodrome, and the Olympic Stadium did. Of the three, the one most in the Fun Palace tradition is Zaha Hadid's Aquatics Centre, whose wavy roof and flexible seating attempt some of what Price attempted. It is very good architecture. It is not the Fun Palace.

docs.title: Plug-in City
docs.text: ArchitectPeter Cook (b. 1936), of the Archigram group Drawn1964, published in Archigram 4 Intended siteGeneric — a city typology intended for eventual application anywhere Height / scaleDiagonal service-lattice megastructure 100–200 m tall; individual dwelling capsules slotted into the lattice Statusunbuilt — influential on later capsule and megastructure projects Diagonal service lattice with plug-in residential and commercial capsules; a crane running on top rail

docs.title: What it was
docs.text:
Peter Cook's Plug-in City is the clearest architectural expression of Archigram's core idea: that the city's permanent infrastructure — services, circulation, structure — should be separate from the city's temporary content — homes, shops, offices. The permanent infrastructure is a megastructure. The temporary content is a catalogue of plug-in capsules.

The megastructure in Cook's drawings is a diagonal lattice of service spines, rising to fifteen or twenty storeys, with horizontal service decks at regular intervals. The diagonal lines carry power, water, waste, data, and circulation. The horizontal decks are the loading zones into which capsules are plugged. Each capsule is a prefabricated unit — a studio apartment, a two-bedroom flat, a shop, a clinic, a classroom — manufactured in a factory and trucked to the city. Cranes running on rails atop the megastructure hoist capsules into place and, when the tenant's lease ends, remove them again.

Cook's published drawings specified depreciation periods for different parts of the city. Water and power infrastructure: forty years. Structural lattice: thirty years. Shops: five years. Dwelling capsules: fifteen years. Single-occupant rooms: three years. The city was designed from the outset to be iteratively replaced, with different lifespans for different components, on a known schedule.

The drawings circulated through Archigram magazine, through the Architectural Association's lectures, and through international publications in the mid-1960s. They appeared in the 1967 Museum of Modern Art show "Architecture without Architects" (though that show focused on vernacular; Archigram's inclusion was by contrast) and in Reyner Banham's influential 1976 book Megastructure.

docs.title: Why it failed
docs.text:
Plug-in City was not a single building proposed to a single client; it was a typology proposed to the discipline. The one mid-sized city in the 1960s that adopted pieces of the Archigram approach was Montreal, for Expo 67, where Moshe Safdie's Habitat 67 built a capsule megastructure at residential scale. Habitat 67 was partially built, stood, and is still occupied — but it is a single building, not a city, and its capsule replacement mechanism was never used.

A larger attempt was Kurokawa's Nakagin Capsule Tower in Tokyo (1972), which built the plug-in capsule idea as a single office-plus-residence building with 140 detachable capsules. The capsules were intended to be replaced every twenty-five years. None ever were. When the building's condition deteriorated irreparably, the decision in 2022 was to demolish the entire tower and preserve twenty-three of the capsules as museum objects. The replacement mechanism — the thing Archigram had designed everything around — turned out to be the feature no institution would actually execute.

The deeper failure mode is that buildings, once built, develop histories. Tenants furnish them, argue with them, attach memories to them. The Archigram premise that dwellings should be swapped out the way cartridges are swapped in and out of game consoles underestimated how much residents want their dwelling to be their dwelling, not an interchangeable unit within an upgrade schedule.

docs.title: What-if
docs.text:
Plug-in City's vocabulary — prefabricated modular building units, service megastructures, rapid reconfiguration — has been partially absorbed into every subsequent conversation about modular housing. The shipping-container housing movement of the 2000s is a direct descendant. Contemporary developers in China, Japan, and Sweden build residential towers from pre-cast concrete modules delivered on trucks and stacked by crane. The technology Archigram prophesied is now standard. What is missing is the swap-out — the continuous replacement that would make the city genuinely plug-in.

If a city had ever been built to Plug-in logic in full, it would be a strange thing to live in: always under construction, partly yours and partly institutionally-managed, upgraded on a schedule like a software release. It would also probably be cheaper to house people in than any city we have built. The underlying economic logic of industrial production — that unit cost falls with volume — applies to housing capsules as well as it applies to cars or phones. The reason housing costs have risen faster than other consumer goods over the past fifty years is, in part, that housing has refused industrialisation in the Plug-in sense. Archigram saw this coming. No one has taken them up on the remedy.

docs.title: Tokyo Bay Plan
docs.text: ArchitectKenzō Tange (1913–2005), with his MIT graduate-student team Designed1960; presented at the World Design Conference, Tokyo, and in Tange's *A Plan for Tokyo, 1960* Intended siteTokyo Bay — a linear axis extending from the Ginza district south across the water to the Chiba peninsula Height / scaleApproximately 80 km linear spine; population capacity ~10 million on branching A-frame residential units Statusunbuilt — partial influence on later bay developments Central highway spine on piers, with A-frame residential megastructures branching above

docs.title: What it was
docs.text:
In 1960 Kenzō Tange presented A Plan for Tokyo, 1960 at the World Design Conference in Tokyo. The plan addressed what the conference had convened to discuss: the unmanageable growth of Japan's capital city, which had recovered from wartime destruction and was now expanding faster than any urban-planning framework could contain. Tokyo had historically grown by accretion around the Imperial Palace. Tange proposed it instead grow linearly, across the water of Tokyo Bay.

The plan is organised around a spine: a double ribbon of elevated highway, running on concrete piers across the bay from the existing city centre to the Chiba peninsula, approximately 80 kilometres long. At intervals along the spine, A-frame megastructures rise above the highway. Each A-frame is a lattice of residential decks, stepping inward as the frame rises to its apex. Offices, shops, and public facilities are integrated into the frames at various heights. The bay itself — the water between the piers — remains navigable; ships pass beneath the spine.

The plan is the founding document of Metabolism, the Japanese architectural movement that dominated the 1960s. Metabolism took as its premise that cities should be designed to grow and to shed cells — new residential capsules plugged in, old ones removed, infrastructure replaced in pieces — the way biological organisms grow. The Tokyo Bay Plan is the most complete expression of that idea at urban scale. Each A-frame can be extended; new A-frames can be added along the spine as the city's population grows; old sections can be demolished without affecting the whole.

Tange and his MIT-trained team (including Arata Isozaki and Kisho Kurokawa, who would go on to their own distinguished careers) worked out the scheme at a level of detail rare for a speculative project. Population projections were run; traffic models were built; concrete consumption was estimated; administrative jurisdictions were proposed.

docs.title: Why it failed
docs.text:
Tokyo in 1960 was governed by a plural patchwork of wards, each with its own interests, and none of them had the authority to commission an 80-kilometre megastructure across Tokyo Bay. The national government did not undertake urban-scale speculative projects on that scale; the bay was in any case being used for harbours, industry, and landfill, and the plan would have displaced these uses.

What Tokyo did instead was build piecemeal onto the bay. Starting in the 1960s and accelerating through the 1980s and 1990s, the Tokyo Bay shoreline was extended by progressive reclamation — Odaiba, the Rainbow Bridge area, and Tokyo Bay Aqua-Line, the tunnel-and-bridge crossing of the bay completed in 1997. These developments took place without the coordinating spine Tange proposed. They are additive, not planned; they are the bay made into land, rather than the bay made into a city.

docs.title: What-if
docs.text:
If Tokyo had adopted Tange's plan, the capital city would be a 80-kilometre line rather than a 40-kilometre disc. Transport between the northern and southern ends of the city would be fast along the spine and slow perpendicular to it. The A-frame residential blocks would have become the dominant housing type, producing a city where perhaps three-quarters of residents lived in megastructures with shared infrastructure, and the rest in traditional low-rise.

The Metabolist promise of the plan — that cells could be added and removed, that buildings could evolve — was never seriously tested at urban scale. The one Metabolist building that did get completed, Kurokawa's Nakagin Capsule Tower (1972), was demolished in 2022 because its capsules had never been swapped out as intended. The tower rusted in place and was replaced, not upgraded. This is the practical difficulty with Metabolism: the replacement mechanism requires institutional continuity that cities do not tend to provide.

Tange's later career produced built work at similar scale — the Yoyogi gymnasiums, the Tokyo Government Building in Shinjuku — none of it with the bay plan's radical geometry. The Tokyo we have is the Tokyo that grew by accretion around the Imperial Palace, with Tange's buildings distributed through it as individual nodes. The Tokyo we do not have is the line across the bay.

docs.title: Walking City
docs.text: ArchitectRon Herron (1930–1994), of the Archigram group Drawn1964, published in Archigram issue 5 Intended siteBy design, none — the city walks from place to place Height / scaleApproximately 200 m long capsule bodies on telescoping legs; no specified passenger capacity Statusunbuilt — intentionally provocative Two bug-like megastructures on telescoping legs, crossing a distant skyline

docs.title: What it was
docs.text:
Archigram was a loose collective of six young British architects — Warren Chalk, Peter Cook, Dennis Crompton, David Greene, Ron Herron, Mike Webb — who met at the Architectural Association in London in the early 1960s and produced a magazine of the same name from 1961 to 1974. Archigram published drawings, manifestos, and photomontages of radical new building types: Plug-in cities, cushicles (inflatable dwellings), instant cities, urban robots. Most of it was drawn, almost none of it was built. The drawings themselves were the point.

The Walking City, by Ron Herron, appeared in Archigram 5 in 1964. The drawing shows enormous ovoid building-bodies — each perhaps 200 metres long, supported on eight telescoping legs — traversing a landscape that is identifiably somewhere between New York and the sea. The cities are insectoid, mechanical, clearly alive. Inside each body are dwellings, workplaces, recreation: the full programme of a small town, about 6,000 people. On the outer surface, rows of portholes; on the top, chimneys and communications masts; underneath, the legs, which telescope for walking and for settling.

The proposition was that the city should become mobile. A Walking City at Sydney on Monday could be in San Francisco on Friday. It could dock against another Walking City, or against a conventional city, by extending temporary bridges between hulls. It could wade offshore in a flood. It could leave a place when the resources of that place ran out. It was the opposite of every idea of a city up to that date — the settled city, the rooted city, the permanent city.

docs.title: Why it failed
docs.text:
The Walking City was not submitted to a planning authority and was never expected to be built. Archigram's drawings were editorial: they were meant to shake the discipline of architecture out of what the group saw as the deadening post-war compromise between modernist utopia and municipal rationalism. The drawings were themselves the output. They were shown at the Whitechapel Gallery, at the Paris Biennale, at the Museum of Modern Art. They are now in museum collections across the world.

Could a Walking City be engineered? Mechanically, yes — the telescoping-leg mechanism is tractable at reasonable scale; small mobile structures of similar principle exist (the Bagger 288 bucket-wheel excavator, the Apollo Crawler-Transporter). Nothing Herron drew violates physics. What it violates is the economic logic of buildings. A building that moves is more expensive per unit of space than a building that does not move. There is no obvious commercial market for a city that walks. The only customers would be circuses, armies, and mining companies, and each of those has settled for less ambitious solutions.

docs.title: What-if
docs.text:
A successful Walking City would have rewritten the idea of "home". People would live somewhere but not live at somewhere. The city would dock, for a week or a month, then walk to its next location. Employment, civic participation, school assignments, postal service — every institution that assumes a fixed residence would have to be reorganised around residential mobility at city scale. We do not know what such a society would look like because we have never produced it.

Archigram's larger insight — that buildings might not need to be permanent, that architecture could be considered the organisation of change rather than the creation of fixity — has had a diffuse influence on the discipline. Buckminster Fuller's Dymaxion House shares it; Yona Friedman's Spatial Cities share it; Price's Fun Palace shares it. None of these got built. The buildings that did get built since 1964 are, with rare exceptions, as permanent as buildings have always been.

The Walking City is worth revisiting now because climate-driven population movement is beginning to make mobility at urban scale a live question. Some coastal Bangladeshi villages have been moving inland at a rate of tens of metres per year. Some Alaskan villages have been relocating entirely. The form these moves take is not insectoid megastructures; it is, typically, resettlement to new concrete-and-steel buildings in safer places. The underlying phenomenon — that the built environment must sometimes migrate — is nonetheless one Archigram noticed sixty years early.

docs.title: The Tower of Babel
docs.text: ArchitectPieter Bruegel the Elder (painter; the "architect" is the biblical Nimrod) Painted1563 (Vienna version); second version c. 1568 (Rotterdam) Intended siteShinar; Bruegel transposes it onto a harbour that reads as Antwerp Height / scaleBruegel's tower reads at approximately 500 metres — far taller than any building of 1563, or 2026 Statusimagined — abandoned by God Seven stepped drums, a spiral ramp, and the famously unfinished top

docs.title: What it was
docs.text:
Genesis 11 gives the tower a single sentence of description: the people of Shinar resolved to build "a city, and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven." Everything else — its form, its engineering, its colour, its ruin — has been supplied by painters. Bruegel's Vienna Tower of Babel, painted in 1563, is the painting that most people mean when they picture the building. It is the canonical Babel.

The design is a seven-drum stepped cylinder, each drum smaller than the one beneath, wrapped by a continuous spiral ramp along which tiny figures haul tiny stones. The lower drums are built in a Roman arcaded masonry recognisable from the Colosseum; the higher drums shift toward rougher fabrications. At the very top, the construction breaks down mid-air, with scaffolds and half-raised blocks. The painting is in the middle of construction forever.

Bruegel places the tower at the edge of a working port. Ships are moored at the base. Cranes are operating. In the foreground the king — Nimrod — inspects the work with his retinue while masons bow. The painter has transposed a biblical scene onto the Low Countries of his day, and the tower stands as a project that Antwerp's merchants could plausibly have commissioned if they'd had the labour and the hubris.

docs.title: Why it failed
docs.text:
The scriptural reason: language. God, displeased with the project's presumption, confused the tongues of the builders; they could no longer coordinate; the tower was abandoned. The reason the tower remains unbuilt in any subsequent era is structural. No masonry compression tower of the proportions Bruegel paints can stand: the load at the base would exceed the compressive strength of the stone long before the upper drums rose. The tower in the painting is already failing — the drums are visibly out of plumb, and cracks run through the lower courses. Bruegel knew this. He was painting a ruin-in-progress.

The choice of cloud level is itself a kind of admission. The upper drums disappear into a layer of mist. We never see the top. The building's crown is literally beyond depiction.

docs.title: What-if
docs.text:
If the Tower of Babel existed, it would be what Boullée's cenotaph and Tatlin's spiral attempt to be: a building whose size is the message, independent of function. The iconography of the colossal — Lenin on Iofan's base, Hitler under Speer's dome, Saddam Hussein's Victory Arch — all inherit something from Bruegel's plate, by way of every painter who copied it for four hundred years.

Bruegel's tower is also the first ruin of modernity. The building does not die from age; it dies from ambition. The stones are fresh. The cranes are still turning. The building has simply been too large to build for as long as anyone has tried to imagine such a building, and it will remain so.

docs.title: Da Vinci's Ideal City
docs.text: ArchitectLeonardo da Vinci (1452–1519) Designedc. 1487, sketched across several folios of the Paris MS B Intended siteProposed for Milan following the plague of 1484–1485 Height / scaleCity for approximately 30,000 inhabitants on two circulation levels Statusunbuilt Two-level section: arcaded upper streets, service canal and lower streets beneath

docs.title: What it was
docs.text:
Leonardo's ideal city does not exist as a single drawing. It appears in fragments across the folios of Paris Manuscript B — plans, sections, elevations, notes on sewage, notes on water supply, notes on loading bays. Assembled, these fragments describe a city organised on two levels.

The upper level is for the rich. It is reached by a continuous arcaded street at first-floor height and is reserved for pedestrians, for horses ridden for pleasure, and for carriages bearing gentlemen. Buildings line the upper street with their principal facades. Windows and balconies open outward to the arcade. The proportions are Vitruvian, the materials stone.

The lower level is for everyone and everything else. Beneath the arcaded street runs a deeper street for carts, for porters, for deliveries. Beneath that, in a channel cut parallel to the lower street, runs a canal. The canal takes goods in and takes waste out. The lower level is connected to the upper by stairs placed at frequent intervals, and the upper is connected to the lower by chutes through which the refuse of the houses falls directly into the canal below.

The design was Leonardo's response to the plague that killed as much as a third of Milan's population between 1484 and 1485. He blamed the disease on the filth of the existing streets — on the mixing of commerce, traffic, animals, and people in the narrow medieval lanes of the city. His solution was spatial separation: to lift the citizens up out of the muck on a clean level, and to push the muck down onto a working level beneath them.

docs.title: Why it failed
docs.text:
Milan did not have the money, and Ludovico Sforza — Leonardo's patron, and Francesco's son — had other wars to fight. The plan required demolishing large parts of the existing city and rebuilding on a uniform geometric grid with uniform facades. No Renaissance duke ever had that kind of authority over his own capital. Even Haussmann, who did have something approaching that authority four centuries later, could only rebuild arterial corridors through Paris, not the whole city.

There is also a social objection that Leonardo's plan raises and does not resolve. The two-level scheme makes the class hierarchy of the city into an architectural hierarchy. The rich walk over the heads of the poor, and the poor never need to appear to the rich. Later ideal cities retained the hygienic insight — separate the waste from the citizenry — without the social one. The London sewer system of the 1860s, Paris's Haussmann sewers of the 1850s, and every modern city's underground infrastructure, are Leonardo's lower level built without the upper.

docs.title: What-if
docs.text:
If Leonardo had been given Milan to rebuild, the model for every nineteenth-century sewer system would have been Italian rather than French or English. The social geometry of the plan would likely not have survived: cities built on class-stratified levels do not remain so for long. The canal beneath would have served as a hybrid drain-and-delivery system, with consequences for hygiene that the rest of Europe would have had to catch up to.

The lingering insight of Leonardo's plan is that infrastructure is part of architecture. A building whose service entrances, waste outlets, and delivery routes are designed into the original section is a different building from one whose infrastructure is bolted on later. Most of the modern buildings around you are the bolted-on kind. Leonardo drew, in 1487, the other kind.

docs.title: Sforzinda
docs.text: ArchitectAntonio di Pietro Averlino, called Filarete (c. 1400 – c. 1469) Designed1457–1464, described in the *Trattato di architettura* Intended siteThe Duchy of Milan, at the pleasure of Francesco Sforza. Never sited. Height / scaleCity for approximately 100,000 inhabitants on an eight-pointed star plan inscribed in a circle of ~3.5 km diameter Statusunbuilt Eight-pointed star plan with eight radial streets converging on a central piazza

docs.title: What it was
docs.text:
Sforzinda is the first complete design for an ideal city in Western architecture. Filarete drew it for Francesco Sforza, the condottiere-turned-Duke of Milan whose name the city was to carry. The plan is an eight-pointed star — two squares rotated forty-five degrees from each other — set inside a moat. Eight radial streets run from the points of the star to a central piazza. The eight valleys between the star's points hold markets and minor squares; the eight bastions of the points hold defensive towers.

At the centre sits a complex of three piazzas: the principal square with the Duke's palace and the cathedral, and two flanking squares for the markets and for the Courts of Justice. From the central piazza rises the Casa della Virtù e del Vizio — the House of Virtue and Vice — a stepped tower whose lower floors contain brothels and gaming rooms and whose upper floors contain schools of music, rhetoric, and astronomy. The inhabitant of the lower floors, by climbing the tower, literally ascends from vice to virtue. Filarete's illustrations show each floor in elevation.

The treatise that describes Sforzinda is the Trattato di architettura, a manuscript of more than three hundred folios in dialogue form. It is a weird book. It contains Filarete's plans for the city's hospitals (radial wards for contagion control, a form the 19th century would eventually rediscover), its sewer system, its prison, and its harbour, along with astrological charts for siting the foundation stones. The whole city is set according to the positions of the planets on a specified date.

docs.title: Why it failed
docs.text:
Sforzinda failed because Sforza's Milan did not want a new city; it wanted to strengthen the city it had. Filarete arrived in Milan in 1451 as a builder with an existing reputation — he had cast the bronze doors of St Peter's in Rome — and Sforza employed him on the Ospedale Maggiore, which was built and survives. The ideal-city treatise was a side project, presented to the Duke as a proposal but never acted on. Sforza's interests were in strengthening the Castello Sforzesco, paying mercenary armies, and keeping the French out of Lombardy. Founding a new city from nothing for one hundred thousand inhabitants required a peace and a treasury Milan did not possess.

The specific obstacle was money. Filarete's estimate for the founding of Sforzinda runs to figures the Duchy's revenues could not service without taxing itself into revolt. The treatise implicitly assumes a patron with the resources of a monarch and the ambition of a god.

docs.title: What-if
docs.text:
The ideal-city tradition Filarete inaugurated — the star plan, the radial streets, the central piazza — did get built, eventually, but not for Francesco Sforza. Palmanova (founded 1593 by the Venetian Republic as a frontier fortress) is the closest realisation of Sforzinda's military geometry. The planned colonial capitals of the New World — Mannheim, Karlsruhe, L'Enfant's Washington — carried pieces of the scheme forward.

But an intact Sforzinda would have been the first conceptually modern city: every element situated by reason, nothing by historical accident. It would have been a Renaissance rehearsal for Brasília and Chandigarh. The uncomfortable thing about Sforzinda is that Filarete had the idea five hundred years before the tools existed to execute it, and when the tools existed, the cities we built were Brasília and Chandigarh. The inhabitants of those twentieth-century ideal cities did not, on the whole, enjoy them.
